title: Photocatalytic removal of textile wastewater-originated methylene blue and malachite green dyes using spent black tea ex

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section, 'Optimization of salt concentration for SBT-AgNPs'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text first states 'the peak correlated to 50 mM showed at 417 nm while the peak correlating to 100 mM redshifted to 423 nm, implying that particle size has increase[d]' (i.e., two different peak wavelengths), but in the very next sentence claims 'The peaks are a perfect dome shaped with the same high points at same wavelength of 423 nm.' These two statements directly contradict each other regarding whether the 50 mM and 100 mM peaks occur at the same or different wavelengths.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section, 'The optimization of reaction time for the synthesis of SBT-AgNPs'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text reports 'The peak linked with 90 min has an absorption density of 2.9 while the peak of 60 min has ascent rise of 2.6,' meaning 90 min produced a higher absorption signal (more nanoparticles, per the paper's own logic used elsewhere for salt/biomass optimization). Yet the paper concludes 'it can be safely assumed that 60 min time was more efficient than the 90 min reaction time' and selects 60 min as the final optimized condition, which contradicts the higher absorbance observed at 90 min and the cited literature (Li et al.) stating longer reaction time yields better crystallinity.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section, 'Zeta potential analysis is done to estimate the stability of AgNPs'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paragraph states 'the observed zeta potential was -13.6 mV for chemically synthesized AgNPs... and SBT-AgNPs... were observed to be -17.5 mV with zeta deviation of 10.8 and -13.7 mV,' giving two different values (-13.6 mV and -13.7 mV) for the same chemically synthesized AgNP sample within the same paragraph, which is an internal numerical inconsistency.

The paper claims 'As per our knowledge, it is only study which has used spent black tea to synthesize the AgNPs,' yet the Methods section explicitly states the AgNP synthesis protocol was 'conducted by using method previously described by Qing et al. in his study on AgNPs formation from waste tea extract,' directly contradicting the claimed novelty of using spent tea to synthesize AgNPs.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section, discussion following reaction time optimization ('The chemically synthesized AgNPs also showed their characteristic peak at 310 nm')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A characteristic surface plasmon resonance (SPR) peak for silver nanoparticles (including citrate-reduced AgNPs) is well established in the literature to occur around 400–450 nm, not 310 nm. Reporting 310 nm as the 'characteristic peak' for chemically synthesized AgNPs is inconsistent with the SPR behavior described for all other AgNP samples in this same study (reported at 423–425 nm).

The SBT-AgNPs XRD peaks are reported at 38.3°, 40.8°, 64.5°, 74.2° and assigned to (111), (200), (220), (311) planes referencing JCPDS 04-0783, while the chemically synthesized AgNPs (same paper, same reference card) are reported at 38.1°, 44.3°, 64.4°, 81.5° for the identical set of planes. Standard Ag reference values (JCPDS 04-0783) place (200) near 44.3° and (311) near 77.5°, not 40.8°/74.2° as claimed for SBT-AgNPs. The large discrepancy between the two samples' peak positions assigned to the same plane indices from the same reference card indicates a misattribution/inconsistency.

The abstract states the malachite green reduction (33.3% and 60%) 'was remarkably significant owing to the presence of the complex factor in the natural environment,' but no statistical test (p-value, confidence interval, replicate analysis) is reported anywhere in the paper to support a claim of statistical or practical 'significance.'

predicted_errors.error_location: Results/Discussion section on zeta potential and SEM, citing Parvathalu et al. and Goyal et al.
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'The presence of clear zone indicates the inhibition of bacterial growth by nanoparticles... Although, all the samples were plate-like nanoparticles, but they differ in their size and edges and hence show different antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria,' implying the study's own SBT-AgNP and chemically synthesized AgNP samples exhibited differential antibacterial activity. However, no antibacterial assay (zone of inhibition test, bacterial culture, etc.) was described anywhere in the Methods, making this an unsupported claim about the study's own samples based on unrelated cited work.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph on black tea consumption
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim 'According to Pakistan Bureau of Statistics Report (2017), every Pakistani consume 15 kg of black tea annually' is implausible; even the world's highest per-capita tea consuming nations (e.g., Turkey) consume roughly 3 kg per year, making a 15 kg/year claim for Pakistan (commonly cited at ~1-1.5 kg/year) an order of magnitude too high, suggesting a misattributed or fabricated statistic.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, 'Preparation of standard dye of methylene blue and malachite green'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The methylene blue calibration standards were described as being 'prepared from stock solution of 30 mg/L,' but the subsequent degradation experiment uses 'standard dye of methylene blue (0.05 mg/ml)' which equals 50 mg/L — a concentration higher than the stated 30 mg/L stock solution. It is not possible to dilute a 30 mg/L stock to obtain a 50 mg/L working solution without additional undocumented concentration steps, representing an internally inconsistent/impossible protocol.
